0.title: A Farewell Letter from the Rock
0.overview:
Second Peter is the apostle's last will and testament. Writing in the shadow of his own death — 'the putting off of my body will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me' (1:14; cf. John 21:18–19) — Peter addresses a church under pressure from false teachers who have crept inside the community, twisted Paul's letters, and weaponized a crude uniformitarianism against the hope of Christ's return. The letter's three movements answer three threats: the erosion of moral seriousness (ch. 1: grow in the divine nature), the corruption of doctrine by immoral teachers (ch. 2: their condemnation is certain), and the mocking of eschatological hope (ch. 3: the Day is coming and it will be unlike anything the world has seen).

The letter's authorship is the most contested in the NT canon. The vocabulary differs sharply from 1 Peter, and Origen already noted that some doubted it. Eusebius placed it among the antilegomena — letters known but disputed. Yet the arguments for Petrine authorship are substantial: the self-identification is unusually specific (Simeon Peter, v.1; the eyewitness claim of vv.16–18; the reference to a prior letter in 3:1); a forger who fabricates this much personal detail is extraordinarily bold. The vocabulary difference most likely reflects a different secretary — 1 Peter was written dia Silouanou (through Silvanus, 1 Pet 5:12), while 2 Peter's quite different style may reflect Peter writing without that help, or with another. The church ultimately recognized it as canonical, and its theological weight — the virtue chain, the transfiguration testimony, the patience of God, the new creation — fully justifies that recognition.

The relationship to Jude is unavoidable: 2 Peter 2 and Jude share extensive material (the angels who sinned, Sodom and Gomorrah, the Balaam archetype, waterless clouds, the scoffers of the last days). The majority of scholars believe Peter used Jude (not the reverse), which, if correct, places 2 Peter after Jude and in the mid-to-late 60s AD — consistent with Peter's death under Nero (c. 64–68 AD). Peter does not merely copy Jude; he develops, expands, and re-focuses the material for a church whose crisis has moved from external pressure to internal corruption.

1.title: Partakers of the Divine Nature

1.overview:
Chapter 1 lays the foundation. God’s power has already given believers everything they need for life and godliness (v. 3). On that gift rests the command: make every effort to add to your faith, and so confirm your calling (vv. 5, 10). Gift first, then effort: that is the grammar of grace.

The second half grounds Peter’s message in two witnesses that agree: the apostles saw Christ’s glory at the transfiguration, and the prophetic Scriptures, spoken by men carried along by the Holy Spirit, point to the same Christ and his coming day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Divine Power and Precious Promises
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter writes to believers whose faith is of equal value to his own. God’s power has given them everything for life and godliness, and his promises make them sharers in his holy nature. So they must make every effort to grow in a chain of qualities from faith to love. Those who grow are kept from fruitlessness and confirm that God has called them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Partakers of the Divine Nature

God's power has already granted everything needed for life and godliness. Sharing the divine nature means sharing his holiness, not becoming God — and growth in the qualities of verses 5–7 is how a believer confirms his calling.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter told readers who had seen nothing that their faith was of equal standing with his.

Now: When growth stalls, look first for a memory of forgiveness that has grown dim (v. 9).

verseByVerse.quote: Simeon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who have obtained a faith of equal standing with ours by the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ: May grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simeon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who have obtained a faith of equal standing with ours by the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ: May grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.

Meaning first. 2 Peter 1 lays the foundation for resisting false teachers: true knowledge of Christ, a growing Christian character, and the sure word of Scripture. Peter greets those who share the same precious faith through the righteousness of our God and Saviour Jesus Christ (vv. 1–2). God’s divine power has given us everything we need for life and godliness, through knowing him; through his great promises we share in the divine nature and escape the world’s corruption (vv. 3–4). So believers must make every effort to add to their faith a chain of virtues: goodness, knowledge, self-control, endurance, godliness, brotherly affection and love (vv. 5–7). These keep them fruitful; those who lack them are blind and have forgotten their cleansing (vv. 8–9). So be diligent to confirm your calling and election; then you will never fall, and you will receive a rich welcome into Christ’s eternal kingdom (vv. 10–11). Knowing he will die soon, as Jesus foretold, Peter wants to remind them of these things so they will remember after his death (vv. 12–15). The message is not a myth: Peter and others were eyewitnesses of Christ’s majesty at the Transfiguration and heard the Father’s voice (vv. 16–18). And the prophetic word of Scripture is even more sure, a lamp in a dark place until the day dawns, because no prophecy came from human will; men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit (vv. 19–21).

Setting and background. Peter’s farewell letter, written as he expected to die soon (1:14), probably from Rome around AD 64–68, shortly before his martyrdom under Nero. It addresses the same churches as 1 Peter (3:1). Its main concern is false teachers within the churches who denied Christ’s return and lived immorally (chapters 2–3). Chapter 2 closely parallels the letter of Jude.

Simeon Peter. Key words. “Simeon” (Symeōn): the Hebrew form of Simon, his original name, used also by James in Acts 15:14. Peter (Petros, rock): the name Jesus gave him.

A servant and apostle of Jesus Christ. Key words. “Servant” (doulos, slave): humility. “Apostle” (apostolos): authority. Both together.

To those who have obtained a faith of equal standing with ours. Key words. “Obtained” (lachousin, received by lot, been allotted, as a gift). Faith is God’s gift, not earned (Ephesians 2:8). “Of equal standing” (isotimon, equally precious, of the same value, same honour). The faith of these later believers, mostly Gentiles who never saw Jesus, is as precious as the faith of the apostles who walked with him. There is no first-class and second-class Christianity.

By the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ. Key words. “Righteousness” (dikaiosynē): God’s fairness in giving equal faith to all, and the righteousness of Christ by which believers are justified. “Our God and Savior Jesus Christ”: as in Titus 2:13, one article governs both nouns, so that Jesus Christ is called both God and Saviour. Compare 1:11; 2:20; 3:18, where the same construction (“our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ”) clearly refers to one person. A clear statement of Christ’s deity.

May grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord. Key words. “Knowledge” (epignōsei, full, personal, experiential knowledge). A key word of 2 Peter (1:2, 3, 8; 2:20). The false teachers claimed special knowledge; Peter points to the true knowledge of God in Christ, through which grace and peace grow.

Textual note. 2 Peter was the most disputed book in the early church, and many modern scholars doubt that Peter wrote it, pointing to its different style from 1 Peter and its similarity to Jude. But the letter explicitly claims to be from Peter, refers to the Transfiguration as an eyewitness (vv. 16–18), mentions Jesus’ prediction of Peter’s death (v. 14), and refers to a previous letter (3:1). Differences of style may be due to different secretaries (Silvanus helped with 1 Peter, 5:12) and different subjects. The early church, after careful consideration, received it into the canon. We receive it as Peter’s, and as Scripture.

What it does not mean. “Equal standing” does not mean all believers have the same apostolic authority. It means the same saving faith, equally precious to God.

In a sentence. From Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, to those who through the righteousness of our God and Saviour Jesus Christ have received a faith as precious as ours: grace and peace be yours in abundance through the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.

For worship. Thank God that your faith is just as precious as the apostles’ faith, a gift from your God and Saviour Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Peter’s farewell letter, written as he expected to die soon (1:14), probably from Rome in the mid 60s AD. “Simeon” is the Hebrew form of his name.

verseByVerse.quote: His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us to his own glory and excellence, by which he has granted to us his precious and very great promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped from the corruption that is in the world because of sinful desire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us to his own glory and excellence, by which he has granted to us his precious and very great promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped from the corruption that is in the world because of sinful desire.

His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness. Key words. “Divine power” (theias dynameōs): Christ’s power, or God’s. “Granted” (dedōrēmenēs, given as a gift, perfect tense: has given and it remains ours). “All things” (panta): everything we need. “Life and godliness”: spiritual life and the godly living that flows from it. We lack nothing necessary for living a godly life (2 Timothy 3:16–17). The false teachers offered something more; Peter says believers already have everything.

Through the knowledge of him who called us. Key words. “Knowledge” (epignōseōs), as in verse 2. “Called” (kalesantos): God’s effectual call. Everything comes through knowing Christ personally, not through secret teachings.

To his own glory and excellence. Key words. “Glory” (doxē) and “excellence” (aretē, virtue, moral excellence, goodness). Either God called us by his glory and excellence (attracted by his beauty), or to share them. Probably both.

By which he has granted to us his precious and very great promises. Key words. “Precious” (timia) and “very great” (megista, greatest). The promises of forgiveness, the Spirit, eternal life, Christ’s return, and the new creation (3:4, 9, 13).

So that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature. Key words. “Partakers” (koinōnoi, sharers, partners). “Divine nature” (theias physeōs). An astonishing phrase. Through God’s promises, believers share in God’s own moral character and life: his holiness, love, goodness. This is the new birth (1 Peter 1:23; John 3:5–6), union with Christ (John 15:4–5), being renewed in his image (Colossians 3:10; Romans 8:29).

Having escaped from the corruption that is in the world because of sinful desire. Key words. “Escaped” (apophygontes, fled from, got away from). “Corruption” (phthoras, decay, moral rot, destruction). “Sinful desire” (epithymia, lust, craving). The world’s rot comes from evil desire (James 1:14–15). Sharing God’s nature means escaping that rot.

Where Christians differ: do believers become divine? Eastern Orthodoxy teaches theosis or deification, in which believers progressively become “gods by grace.” Some modern movements teach that believers become “little gods.” Verdict: Believers share in God’s moral nature (his holiness, love and life) through union with Christ by the Spirit, but they never share in his essence, his deity, or his incommunicable attributes like omnipotence or omniscience. The Creator-creature distinction is never erased. We become like God in character, not God in being (1 John 3:2; 2 Corinthians 3:18).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers become sinless now, or merge into God. It means God’s life is truly in us, transforming us into his likeness.

In a sentence. His divine power has given us everything we need for a godly life through our knowledge of him who called us by his own glory and goodness. Through these he has given us his very great and precious promises, so that through them you may share in the divine nature, having escaped the corruption in the world caused by evil desires.

For worship. Thank God that he has given you everything you need for godliness, and that by his promises you share in his life.

verseByVerse.quote: For this very reason, make every effort to supplement your faith with virtue, and virtue with knowledge, and knowledge with self-control, and self-control with steadfastness, and steadfastness with godliness, and godliness with brotherly affection, and brotherly affection with love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this very reason, make every effort to supplement your faith with virtue, and virtue with knowledge, and knowledge with self-control, and self-control with steadfastness, and steadfastness with godliness, and godliness with brotherly affection, and brotherly affection with love.

For this very reason, make every effort. Key words. “For this very reason”: because God has given you everything (vv. 3–4). God’s gift is the basis for our effort, not a replacement for it. “Make every effort” (spoudēn pasan pareisenenkantes, bringing in all diligence, applying all eagerness). Grace calls for strenuous effort (Philippians 2:12–13).

To supplement your faith with virtue. Key words. “Supplement” (epichorēgēsate, provide generously, add lavishly). The word was used of a wealthy patron who paid for a Greek chorus, supplying everything lavishly. “Faith” is the foundation; seven qualities are built on it, like a ladder. “Virtue” (aretēn, moral excellence, goodness), the same word used of God in verse 3.

And virtue with knowledge. Key words. “Knowledge” (gnōsin, understanding, practical wisdom). Knowing God’s will and how to apply it.

And knowledge with self-control. Key words. “Self-control” (enkrateian, self-mastery, holding oneself in). The false teachers had knowledge without self-control (2:10–14).

And self-control with steadfastness. Key words. “Steadfastness” (hypomonēn, endurance, patience under pressure), as in James 1:3–4.

And steadfastness with godliness. Key words. “Godliness” (eusebeian, reverence for God shown in life).

And godliness with brotherly affection. Key words. “Brotherly affection” (philadelphian, family love for fellow believers).

And brotherly affection with love. Key words. “Love” (agapēn, self-giving love for all, including enemies). The crown of the list (1 Corinthians 13:13; Colossians 3:14). The list begins with faith and ends with love.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we earn salvation by adding virtues. Faith is the gift that saves; these virtues are the growth of a saved life. Nor does it mean each must be achieved before the next; they grow together.

In a sentence. For this very reason, make every effort to add goodness to your faith; and to goodness, knowledge; and to knowledge, self-control; and to self-control, perseverance; and to perseverance, godliness; and to godliness, love for fellow believers; and to that love, love for all.

On a Tuesday. Which of these seven qualities is weakest in your life? Make a deliberate effort to grow in it this week, relying on God’s power.

verseByVerse.quote: For if these qualities are yours and are increasing, they keep you from being ineffective or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. For whoever lacks these qualities is so nearsighted that he is blind, having forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if these qualities are yours and are increasing, they keep you from being ineffective or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. For whoever lacks these qualities is so nearsighted that he is blind, having forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins.

For if these qualities are yours and are increasing. Key words. “Are yours” (hyparchonta, belong to you, are present in you). “Increasing” (pleonazonta, abounding, multiplying). Not static but growing.

They keep you from being ineffective or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. “Ineffective” (argous, idle, useless, lazy). “Unfruitful” (akarpous, barren). Knowledge of Christ is meant to produce fruit (John 15:8; Colossians 1:10).

For whoever lacks these qualities is so nearsighted that he is blind. Key words. “Nearsighted” (myōpazōn, short-sighted, squinting; our word “myopic”). “Blind” (typhlos). He sees only what is close, the present world, and cannot see eternal realities. Spiritual short-sightedness leads to blindness.

Having forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins. Key words. “Forgotten” (lēthēn labōn, having taken forgetfulness). “Cleansed” (katharismou, purification). He has forgotten the gospel, his own forgiveness. Remembering what Christ has done for us is the motive for growth. Forgetting leads to fruitlessness.

What it does not mean. It does not necessarily mean such a person was never cleansed; it describes a professing believer who has lost sight of grace. Whether genuine or not will be shown by whether he returns (v. 10).

In a sentence. For if you possess these qualities in increasing measure, they will keep you from being ineffective and unproductive in your knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. But whoever does not have them is short-sighted and blind, forgetting that they have been cleansed from their past sins.

For worship. Remember today that you have been cleansed from your past sins. Let that memory fuel your growth.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, brothers, be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election, for if you practice these qualities you will never fall. For in this way there will be richly provided for you an entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, brothers, be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election, for if you practice these qualities you will never fall. For in this way there will be richly provided for you an entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

Therefore, brothers, be all the more diligent. Key words. “Be diligent” (spoudasate, make every effort), echoing verse 5. “All the more” (mallon).

To confirm your calling and election. Key words. “Confirm” (bebaian poieisthai, make firm, make sure, establish, a legal term for ratifying a contract). “Calling” (klēsin): God’s effectual call. “Election” (eklogēn): God’s eternal choice. Calling is mentioned first because it is how we come to know our election. We cannot make our election more certain to God; it is fixed. But we can make it more certain to ourselves, by growing in the qualities of verses 5–7, which are the evidence of genuine faith.

For if you practice these qualities you will never fall. Key words. “Practice” (poiountes, keep doing). “Never fall” (ou mē ptaisēte pote, a strong double negative: you will certainly never stumble). Not that you will never sin, but that you will never fall away, never stumble in the decisive sense, never be lost.

For in this way there will be richly provided for you an entrance into the eternal kingdom. Key words. “Richly provided” (plousiōs epichorēgēthēsetai, lavishly supplied), the same verb as “supplement” (v. 5). As you supply virtues, God will supply a lavish welcome. “Entrance” (eisodos, way in, welcome). Like a victorious athlete or general welcomed home with celebration. “Eternal kingdom”: God’s reign in its fullness.

Of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Key words. The same construction as verse 1: one person, Lord and Saviour.

Where Christians differ: can I know I am elect? Some fear election makes assurance impossible: how can I know if God chose me? Others think assurance comes only by special revelation. Verdict: Believers can and should have assurance of their election. It is grounded first in God’s promises in Christ, received by faith; it is confirmed by the Spirit’s inner witness (Romans 8:16) and by the fruit of a godly life (1 John 2:3; 3:14). Election is not a cause for anxiety but for confidence: those who trust Christ and grow in godliness may know they are chosen (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5). And the elect will persevere: they “will never fall.”

What it does not mean. It does not mean our good works cause our election or our entrance into the kingdom. They confirm it. The kingdom is given by grace.

In a sentence. Therefore, my brothers and sisters, make every effort to confirm your calling and election. For if you do these things, you will never stumble, and you will receive a rich welcome into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ.

For worship. Thank God for calling and choosing you. Ask him to grow these qualities in you, so that your assurance grows too.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–21 — Eyewitnesses and the Prophetic Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter knows he will soon die, as Jesus told him, so he keeps reminding them of what they already know. Their faith does not rest on clever myths: the apostles saw Christ’s majesty and heard the Father’s voice on the mountain. And they have the prophetic word, confirmed by that event, a lamp in a dark place until the day dawns. No prophecy came from the prophet’s own understanding; men spoke from God as the Holy Spirit carried them along.
verseByVerse.theology:
Carried Along

Prophecy did not come from the prophet's own interpretation. Men spoke from God as the Holy Spirit carried them along — fully human, and fully God's word.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter wrote knowing his death was near, and arranged for his readers to remember.

Now: Scripture is a lamp in a dark place — enough light until the day dawns.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I intend always to remind you of these qualities, though you know them and are established in the truth that you have. I think it right, as long as I am in this body, to stir you up by way of reminder, since I know that the putting off of my body will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me. And I will make every effort so that after my departure you may be able at any time to recall these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore I intend always to remind you of these qualities, though you know them and are established in the truth that you have. I think it right, as long as I am in this body, to stir you up by way of reminder, since I know that the putting off of my body will be soon, as our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me. And I will make every effort so that after my departure you may be able at any time to recall these things.

Therefore I intend always to remind you of these qualities. Key words. “Remind” (hypomimnēskein, keep reminding). A key theme (1:12, 13, 15; 3:1–2). Believers do not need new truth; they need to remember old truth.

Though you know them and are established in the truth that you have. Key words. “Established” (estērigmenous, made firm, perfect tense), the word Jesus used when he told Peter to strengthen his brothers (Luke 22:32). Peter is doing exactly that.

I think it right, as long as I am in this body, to stir you up by way of reminder. Key words. “Body” (skēnōmati, tent, tabernacle). A temporary dwelling (2 Corinthians 5:1–4). “Stir you up” (diegeirein, wake up, arouse, keep awake).

Since I know that the putting off of my body will be soon. Key words. “Putting off” (apothesis, laying aside, as one takes off clothing or strikes a tent). Death is a laying aside of the body, not the end of the person.

As our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me. Key words. Jesus had told Peter how he would die (John 21:18–19): when he was old, others would stretch out his hands and lead him where he did not want to go, indicating crucifixion. Tradition says Peter was crucified upside down in Rome under Nero, at his own request, feeling unworthy to die as his Lord had.

And I will make every effort so that after my departure you may be able at any time to recall these things. Key words. “Departure” (exodon, exodus, going out), the word used of Jesus’ death at the Transfiguration (Luke 9:31). Peter’s death is his exodus. “Recall” (mnēmēn poieisthai, remember). Perhaps through this letter, or through Mark’s Gospel, which tradition says records Peter’s preaching.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Peter feared death. He speaks of it calmly as a departure. Nor does it mean believers can do without reminders; even the established need them.

In a sentence. So I will always remind you of these things, even though you know them and are firmly established in the truth you now have. I think it is right to refresh your memory as long as I live in the tent of this body, because I know that I will soon put it aside, as our Lord Jesus Christ has made clear to me. And I will make every effort to see that after my departure you will always be able to remember these things.

For worship. Thank God for those who have reminded you of the gospel. And think about what spiritual legacy you will leave behind.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus had told Peter how he would die.

verseByVerse.quote: For we did not follow cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty. For when he received honor and glory from God the Father, and the voice was borne to him by the Majestic Glory, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased," we ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we did not follow cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty. For when he received honor and glory from God the Father, and the voice was borne to him by the Majestic Glory, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased,” we ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain.

For we did not follow cleverly devised myths. Key words. “Cleverly devised” (sesophismenois, sophisticated, cunningly crafted, made up). “Myths” (mythois, fables, legends). The false teachers apparently accused the apostles of inventing stories about Christ’s return. Peter insists: the gospel is history, not myth.

When we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. “Power and coming” (dynamin kai parousian): probably his powerful second coming, which the false teachers denied (3:4). “Coming” (parousia): his return in glory.

But we were eyewitnesses of his majesty. Key words. “Eyewitnesses” (epoptai, observers, those admitted to see). “Majesty” (megaleiotētos, greatness, magnificence). At the Transfiguration, Peter saw a preview of Christ’s coming glory.

For when he received honor and glory from God the Father. Key words. The Transfiguration (Matthew 17:1–8; Mark 9:2–8; Luke 9:28–36). Jesus’ face shone like the sun, his clothes became dazzling white, and Moses and Elijah appeared.

And the voice was borne to him by the Majestic Glory. Key words. “Majestic Glory” (megaloprepous doxēs, magnificent glory): a reverent way of naming God, perhaps referring to the bright cloud of God’s presence that overshadowed them.

This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased. Key words. The Father’s declaration (Matthew 17:5), echoing Psalm 2:7 and Isaiah 42:1, and the words at Jesus’ baptism (Matthew 3:17).

We ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain. Key words. “We ourselves”: Peter, James and John. “Holy mountain”: the mountain made holy by God’s presence, perhaps Mount Hermon or Mount Tabor. The “holy mountain” is the Mount of Transfiguration, where Peter, James and John saw Jesus glorified. Peter’s testimony is firsthand.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christian faith rests on experiences of glory. Peter will say the prophetic word is even more sure (v. 19). It means the gospel rests on real, historical events witnessed by reliable people.

In a sentence. For when we told you about the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ in power, we were not following cleverly made-up stories, but we had seen his majesty with our own eyes. He received honour and glory from God the Father when the voice came to him from the Majestic Glory, saying, “This is my Son, whom I love; with him I am well pleased.” We ourselves heard this voice that came from heaven when we were with him on the sacred mountain.

For worship. Thank God that your faith rests on facts witnessed by real people. Worship the beloved Son with whom the Father is well pleased.
verseByVerse.note: The “holy mountain” is the Mount of Transfiguration, where Peter, James and John saw Jesus’ glory.

verseByVerse.quote: And we have the prophetic word more fully confirmed, to which you will do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we have the prophetic word more fully confirmed, to which you will do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts,

And we have the prophetic word more fully confirmed. Key words. “Prophetic word” (ton prophētikon logon): the Old Testament Scriptures as a whole, which prophesy Christ, including his coming in glory. “More fully confirmed” (bebaioteron, more sure, more firm, more reliable). Two readings: (1) the Transfiguration confirmed the prophecies, making them even more certain; or (2) the prophetic Scriptures are even more reliable than Peter’s experience. The second fits well with verses 20–21: Scripture is more certain than any experience, even an apostle’s vision, because it comes from God himself.

To which you will do well to pay attention. Key words. “Pay attention” (prosechontes, give heed to, hold the mind on).

As to a lamp shining in a dark place. Key words. “Lamp” (lychnō). “Dark place” (auchmērō topō, a dry, dirty, murky place, squalid). This world, darkened by sin and false teaching, is like a dark, squalid room. Scripture is the lamp that shows the way (Psalm 119:105).

Until the day dawns. Key words. “Day dawns” (hēmera diaugasē, shines through): the day of Christ’s return (Romans 13:12).

And the morning star rises in your hearts. Key words. “Morning star” (phōsphoros, light-bearer, the planet Venus, which announces dawn). Christ himself (Revelation 22:16; Numbers 24:17; Malachi 4:2). “In your hearts”: when Christ returns, believers will know him fully, with full inner illumination (1 Corinthians 13:12). Until then, we need the lamp of Scripture.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Scripture is unnecessary once we have a personal experience of Christ. We need it until he returns. Nor does “dark place” mean Scripture is dim; it is a bright lamp in a dark world.

In a sentence. We also have the prophetic message as something even more reliable, and you will do well to pay attention to it, as to a light shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts.

For worship. Thank God for the lamp of his word in a dark world. Hold it close until Christ, the morning star, comes.

verseByVerse.quote: knowing this first of all, that no prophecy of Scripture comes from someone's own interpretation. For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
knowing this first of all, that no prophecy of Scripture comes from someone’s own interpretation. For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.

Knowing this first of all. Key words. “First of all” (prōton, above all, of first importance).

That no prophecy of Scripture comes from someone’s own interpretation. Key words. “Interpretation” (epilyseōs, explanation, unravelling, solution). Two readings: (1) no prophecy originated in the prophet’s own understanding or explanation of things (it came from God); or (2) no individual may interpret prophecy according to his own private opinion. The next verse supports the first: the point is the origin of Scripture. Prophets did not make up their messages based on their own insight into events.

For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man. Key words. “Produced” (ēnechthē, was brought, carried). Scripture did not begin with human initiative or decision.

But men spoke from God. Key words. “From God” (apo theou): God was the source. Human authors truly spoke, using their own languages, styles and personalities, but the message originated with God.

As they were carried along by the Holy Spirit. Key words. “Carried along” (pheromenoi, borne along, driven), the same word used of a ship driven by the wind (Acts 27:15, 17). The authors were like sailing ships, carried by the wind of the Spirit to the destination God intended. They were active (raising their sails), but the Spirit supplied the power and direction. This is the doctrine of inspiration: Scripture is God-breathed (2 Timothy 3:16), fully human and fully divine in its authorship, so that what Scripture says, God says.

Where Christians differ: is Scripture fully inspired and without error? Some hold that Scripture is inspired only in its religious teaching, or that it contains human errors alongside divine truth. Verdict: Because Scripture came from God through men carried along by the Spirit, it shares God’s truthfulness. It is inerrant in all that it affirms, infallible in its teaching, and sufficient for faith and life. The human authors were not mere typewriters; God used their personalities and research (Luke 1:1–4). But the Spirit so guided them that what they wrote is the very word of God (1 Thessalonians 2:13). Sola Scriptura: Scripture is the final authority over every tradition, experience and claim of revelation.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ordinary believers cannot interpret Scripture. They can and should, carefully and humbly, within the fellowship of the church (Acts 17:11). It means no prophet made up the message himself, and no interpreter may twist Scripture to say what he wants (3:16).

In a sentence. Above all, you must understand that no prophecy of Scripture came about through the prophet’s own interpretation of things. For prophecy never had its origin in human will, but prophets, though human, spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.

For worship. Thank God that Scripture is his word, carried to us by the Spirit. Read it today as God speaking.

1.theology:
The chapter's great theological claim is 'partakers of the divine nature' (v. 4). This is not deification in the Orthodox sense (we do not become God or merge into the divine essence) nor pantheism (we do not become part of God). It is moral participation: through the Spirit and through union with Christ, God's own character — his holiness, patience, love, truthfulness — is communicated to the believer. Calvin read it as a sharing in God's qualities, not in his essence. The Reformed doctrine of sanctification is nothing less than the outworking of this participation: the divine nature expressing itself in human virtue.

The doctrine of Scripture (vv. 20–21) is equally central. Scripture is not a human document about God; it is God's own word spoken through human instruments. The Spirit carried the prophets; therefore the prophets' words carry divine authority. This is why Peter can call the prophetic word 'more fully confirmed' — the written word outlasts the eyewitness, is available to all, and carries the authority not of human testimony but of the Spirit who inspired it.
1.examples:
The virtue chain (vv. 5–7) addresses a perennial pastoral problem: Christians who park at faith and see no need to move. 'I believe — isn't that enough?' Peter's answer: faith is the beginning, not the destination. A Christian who has been given the divine nature and is not building virtue, knowledge, and love is like a person given a magnificent musical instrument who never practices. The gift is real; the neglect is also real; and the result is the same — no music. Note that Peter does not make the virtues the condition of salvation (they flow from faith, not to it) but the evidence of its reality and the trajectory of its growth.

The lamp-and-morning-star image (v. 19) is a pastoral gift for believers who feel that Scripture reading is dry and unproductive. You do not read the Bible because it is always exciting; you read it because you are in a dark place and it is the only lamp available. The darkness is not a reason to put the lamp down. The lamp is precisely what a dark place requires.

2.title: The Anatomy of a False Teacher
2.text: <sup>1</sup>But false prophets also arose among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, bringing upon themselves swift destruction.<sup>2</sup>And many will follow their sensuality, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed.<sup>3</sup>And in their greed they will exploit you with false words. Their condemnation from long ago is not idle, and their destruction is not asleep.<sup>4</sup>For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into hell and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment;<sup>5</sup>if he did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others, when he brought a flood upon the world of the ungodly;<sup>6</sup>if by turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes he condemned them to extinction, making them an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly;<sup>7</sup>and if he rescued righteous Lot, greatly distressed by the sensual conduct of the wicked<sup>8</sup>(for as that righteous man lived among them day after day, he was tormenting his righteous soul over their lawless deeds that he saw and heard);<sup>9</sup>then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment,<sup>10</sup>and especially those who indulge in the lust of defiling passion and despise authority. Bold and willful, they do not tremble as they blaspheme the glorious ones,<sup>11</sup>whereas angels, though greater in might and power, do not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against them before the Lord.<sup>12</sup>But these, like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be caught and destroyed, blaspheming about matters of which they are ignorant, will also be destroyed in their destruction,<sup>13</sup>suffering wrong as the wage for their wrongdoing. They count it pleasure to revel in the daytime. They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their deceptions, while they feast with you.<sup>14</sup>They have eyes full of adultery, insatiable for sin. They entice unsteady souls. They have hearts trained in greed. Accursed children!<sup>15</sup>Forsaking the right way, they have gone astray. They have followed the way of Balaam, the son of Beor, who loved gain from wrongdoing,<sup>16</sup>but was rebuked for his own transgression; a speechless donkey spoke with human voice and restrained the prophet's madness.<sup>17</sup>These are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm. For them the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved.<sup>18</sup>For, speaking loud boasts of folly, they entice by sensual passions of the flesh those who are barely escaping from those who live in error.<sup>19</sup>They promise them freedom, but they themselves are slaves of corruption. For whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved.<sup>20</sup>For if, after they have escaped the defilements of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, the last state has become worse for them than the first.<sup>21</sup>For it would have been better for them never to have known the way of righteousness than after knowing it to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them.<sup>22</sup>What the true proverb says has happened to them: "The dog returns to its own vomit, and the sow, after washing herself, returns to wallow in the mire."
2.overview:
Chapter 2 is Peter’s portrait of the false teacher: his method (slipping in quietly), his doctrine (denying the Master), his motive (greed) and his end (judgment already on its way). Three examples from history, the angels, the flood and Sodom, show that God judges the wicked and rescues the godly. Then Peter describes the teachers themselves: arrogant, driven by appetite, greedy like Balaam, preying on new believers.

The key irony is v. 19: they promise freedom while they themselves are slaves of corruption. The test of a teacher is not the sophistication of his words but the shape of his life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Arrival and Judgment of False Teachers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: False prophets troubled Israel, and false teachers will trouble the church. They bring in destructive heresies, deny the Master who bought them, and exploit people for money. But history shows how God acts: he did not spare the angels who sinned, the ancient world, or Sodom, yet he preserved Noah and rescued Lot. So the Lord knows how to rescue the godly and to hold the wicked for judgment.
verseByVerse.theology:
Righteous Lot

False teachers arise from within. God did not spare the angels, the ancient world or Sodom — yet he preserved Noah and rescued Lot. He knows how to rescue the godly and to hold the unrighteous for judgement.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Lot, compromised as he was, was tormented by the evil he saw day after day.

Now: Being grieved by the world’s evil is a mark of the righteous; being comfortable with it is the danger.

verseByVerse.quote: But false prophets also arose among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, bringing upon themselves swift destruction. And many will follow their sensuality, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed. And in their greed they will exploit you with false words. Their condemnation from long ago is not idle, and their destruction is not asleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But false prophets also arose among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, bringing upon themselves swift destruction. And many will follow their sensuality, and because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed. And in their greed they will exploit you with false words. Their condemnation from long ago is not idle, and their destruction is not asleep.

Meaning first. 2 Peter 2 is a sustained warning against false teachers. As there were false prophets in Israel, so there will be false teachers in the church, who secretly introduce destructive heresies, deny the Master who bought them, lead many into immorality, bring the truth into disrepute, and exploit believers out of greed; their judgement is certain (vv. 1–3). Peter proves it from three examples of past judgement: the angels who sinned, the world of Noah’s day, and Sodom and Gomorrah; and two examples of rescue: Noah and Lot. So the Lord knows how to rescue the godly and to hold the unrighteous for judgement (vv. 4–9). The false teachers are then described in vivid detail: they indulge corrupt desires, despise authority, slander heavenly beings, behave like irrational animals, revel in pleasure, have eyes full of adultery, entice the unstable, and are trained in greed; they follow Balaam, who loved the wages of wrongdoing (vv. 10–16). They are waterless springs and mists driven by storms, promising freedom while they themselves are slaves of corruption (vv. 17–19). Having once escaped the world’s defilements through knowing Christ, they have been entangled again; their last state is worse than the first, like a dog returning to its vomit or a washed pig returning to the mud (vv. 20–22).

Setting and background. Much of this chapter closely parallels the letter of Jude, which may have drawn on 2 Peter or vice versa, or both may have used common material. The false teachers seem to have combined a denial of Christ’s return and future judgement (3:3–4) with moral licence: since there is no judgement coming, live as you please. They may have twisted Paul’s teaching on grace into permission to sin (3:15–16).

But false prophets also arose among the people. Key words. “False prophets” (pseudoprophētai): in Israel’s history, many claimed to speak for God but did not (Deuteronomy 13:1–5; 18:20–22; Jeremiah 23:9–40). Contrast the true prophets of 1:19–21.

Just as there will be false teachers among you. Key words. “False teachers” (pseudodidaskaloi). “Among you”: inside the church, not outside (Acts 20:29–30; Matthew 7:15). The greatest danger often comes from within.

Who will secretly bring in destructive heresies. Key words. “Secretly bring in” (pareisaxousin, smuggle in, slip in alongside). They do not announce their errors openly. “Destructive” (apōleias, of destruction, perdition). “Heresies” (haireseis, choices, factions, sects; later, false teachings that destroy the faith).

Even denying the Master who bought them. Key words. “Denying” (arnoumenoi, disowning, renouncing), by their teaching and their lives (Titus 1:16; Jude 4). “Master” (despotēn, sovereign lord, slave-owner). “Bought” (agorasanta, purchased, as slaves in a market). The language of redemption (1 Corinthians 6:20; Revelation 5:9).

Bringing upon themselves swift destruction. Key words. “Swift” (tachinēn, quick, sudden). Their destruction will come suddenly.

And many will follow their sensuality. Key words. “Sensuality” (aselgeiais, unrestrained immorality, shameless excess). False teaching usually leads to false living.

And because of them the way of truth will be blasphemed. Key words. Way of truth: Christianity (Acts 9:2). “Blasphemed” (blasphēmēthēsetai, slandered). Outsiders will judge Christianity by these people’s behaviour (Romans 2:24).

And in their greed they will exploit you with false words. Key words. “Greed” (pleonexia, covetousness). “Exploit” (emporeusontai, make merchandise of, trade in; our word “emporium”). They treat believers as goods for profit. “False words” (plastois logois, fabricated, made-up words; our word “plastic”).

Their condemnation from long ago is not idle, and their destruction is not asleep. Key words. “From long ago” (ekpalai): God has long since pronounced judgement on such people (Jude 4). “Not idle” (ouk argei, not lazy, not inactive). “Not asleep” (ou nystazei, not dozing). Judgement may seem delayed, but it is wide awake and on its way.

Where Christians differ: does “the Master who bought them” prove Christ died for everyone, including those who perish? Arminians and some others cite this verse to argue that Christ paid for the sins of all, including false teachers who are finally lost. Verdict: Several points apply. The word is “Master” (despotēs), not “Saviour” or “Redeemer”; it pictures a slave-owner who has purchased slaves, and the false teachers deny his rightful ownership. Peter may be speaking of their own profession: they claimed to be bought by Christ and part of the church, and Peter describes them according to that profession, as one might speak of a church member. Or he may be echoing Deuteronomy 32:6, where Israel as a nation is said to have been “bought” by God, though many Israelites were not saved. The verse does not use the language of effective redemption from sin (as in 1 Peter 1:18–19). Scripture elsewhere teaches that Christ laid down his life for his sheep (John 10:11, 15), that his death actually secures the salvation of those for whom he died (Romans 8:32–34; Hebrews 10:14), and that the sheep are never lost (John 10:28). The best reading is that the false teachers professed to belong to the Master who purchased the church, and their denial exposed that profession as false.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every theological disagreement is a destructive heresy. Peter is speaking of denying Christ, combined with immoral living and greed.

In a sentence. But there were also false prophets among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you. They will secretly introduce destructive heresies, even denying the sovereign Lord who bought them, bringing swift destruction on themselves. Many will follow their depraved conduct and will bring the way of truth into disrepute. In their greed these teachers will exploit you with stories they have made up. Their condemnation has long been hanging over them, and their destruction has not been sleeping.

On a Tuesday. Watch for teaching that slips in quietly and leads to immorality or greed. Test every teacher by Scripture and by the fruit of their lives.
verseByVerse.note: Much of this chapter closely parallels the letter of Jude.

verseByVerse.quote: For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into hell and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment; if he did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others, when he brought a flood upon the world of the ungodly; if by turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes he condemned them to extinction, making them an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly;
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but cast them into hell and committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment; if he did not spare the ancient world, but preserved Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others, when he brought a flood upon the world of the ungodly; if by turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes he condemned them to extinction, making them an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly;

For if God did not spare angels when they sinned. Key words. The first of three examples of judgement. “Did not spare” (ouk epheisato). Even angels, the highest creatures, were judged. Which angels? Either the original rebellion of Satan and his angels, or, as Jewish tradition held, the “sons of God” who sinned with human women before the flood (Genesis 6:1–4; Jude 6–7). The order (angels, then the flood, then Sodom) follows Genesis, which suggests the Genesis 6 sin.

But cast them into hell. Key words. “Hell” here is Tartarus (tartarōsas, having cast into Tartarus), a Greek term for the deepest place of punishment, lower than Hades. Peter uses a term his readers would understand for the place of confinement for fallen angels.

And committed them to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment. Key words. “Chains” (seirais, ropes, chains; some manuscripts read sirois, pits). “Gloomy darkness” (zophou, deep gloom). “Kept” (tēroumenous, guarded, held). They are imprisoned now, awaiting final judgement (Jude 6; Revelation 20:10). Not all demons are bound, since many are active (Ephesians 6:12); these particular angels are.

If he did not spare the ancient world. Key words. The second example: the flood (Genesis 6–8).

But preserved Noah, a herald of righteousness, with seven others. Key words. “Preserved” (ephylaxen, guarded, protected). The first example of rescue. “Herald of righteousness” (dikaiosynēs kēryka, preacher of righteousness): Noah warned his generation, as Jewish tradition also held (1 Peter 3:20). “With seven others”: literally “the eighth,” Noah and seven others (his wife, three sons and their wives).

When he brought a flood upon the world of the ungodly. Key words. “Ungodly” (asebōn, irreverent, without regard for God). The whole world except one family.

If by turning the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes he condemned them to extinction. Key words. The third example (Genesis 19). “Turning to ashes” (tephrōsas, reducing to ash). Their sins included sexual immorality and violence (Genesis 19:4–9; Jude 7), pride, excess and neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49–50).

Making them an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly. Key words. “Example” (hypodeigma, pattern, warning). Past judgements are previews of the final judgement (Luke 17:26–30).

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is quick to judge. He waited patiently in Noah’s day (1 Peter 3:20) and would have spared Sodom for ten righteous people (Genesis 18:32). But his judgement does come.

In a sentence. For if God did not spare angels when they sinned, but sent them to the deepest pit, putting them in chains of darkness to be held for judgement; if he did not spare the ancient world when he brought the flood on its ungodly people, but protected Noah, a preacher of righteousness, and seven others; if he condemned the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah by burning them to ashes, and made them an example of what is going to happen to the ungodly;

For worship. Thank God that he is just, and that he also rescues. Pray for those around you who are living as though there were no judgement.
verseByVerse.note: “Hell” here is Tartarus, a Greek term for the deepest place of punishment.

verseByVerse.quote: and if he rescued righteous Lot, greatly distressed by the sensual conduct of the wicked (for as that righteous man lived among them day after day, he was tormenting his righteous soul over their lawless deeds that he saw and heard); then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment,
verseByVerse.commentary:
and if he rescued righteous Lot, greatly distressed by the sensual conduct of the wicked (for as that righteous man lived among them day after day, he was tormenting his righteous soul over their lawless deeds that he saw and heard); then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials, and to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment,

And if he rescued righteous Lot. Key words. The second example of rescue. “Rescued” (errysato, delivered, drew out). “Righteous Lot”: surprising, since Lot made poor choices (Genesis 13:10–13; 19:8, 30–38). But he was righteous by faith, as Abraham was, and God rescued him (Genesis 19:15–16, 29).

Greatly distressed by the sensual conduct of the wicked. Key words. “Greatly distressed” (kataponoumenon, worn down, oppressed, exhausted). “Sensual conduct” (aselgeia, shameless immorality). “Wicked” (athesmōn, lawless, unprincipled).

For as that righteous man lived among them day after day, he was tormenting his righteous soul over their lawless deeds. Key words. Genesis does not tell of Lot’s inner distress, though Lot did protest the men’s demands (Genesis 19:7). Peter, by inspiration, reveals what Lot felt. “Tormenting” (ebasanizen, torturing, vexing). Living in a wicked culture grieved him. Believers today should likewise be grieved, not entertained, by the wickedness around them.

Then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials. Key words. The conclusion of the long sentence (vv. 4–9). “Knows how” (oiden): he has the wisdom and power. “Rescue” (rhyesthai), as with Lot. “Godly” (eusebeis, reverent). “Trials” (peirasmou, testing). God will deliver his people, as he delivered Noah and Lot.

And to keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment. Key words. “Keep” (tērein, hold in custody). “Under punishment” (kolazomenous, being punished, present participle). The wicked who have died are already experiencing punishment, held for the final judgement (Luke 16:23–24). This supports a conscious intermediate state for the wicked as well as for the righteous.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will always be rescued from suffering in this life. It means God will finally rescue them, through death if necessary, and will never abandon them.

In a sentence. and if he rescued Lot, a righteous man, who was distressed by the depraved conduct of the lawless (for that righteous man, living among them day after day, was tormented in his righteous soul by the lawless deeds he saw and heard), then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and to hold the unrighteous for punishment on the day of judgement.

For worship. If you are grieved by the wickedness around you, take heart: the Lord knows how to rescue you.
verseByVerse.note: Genesis does not tell of Lot’s inner distress, though Lot did call the men’s intent wicked (Gen 19:7); Peter draws out the inner side of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–22 — The Portrait, and the Washed Sow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The false teachers scoff at spiritual powers that even angels treat with reverence. They act on instinct like animals, feast at the church’s meals while full of lust and greed, and follow Balaam, who loved money from wrongdoing. They are dry springs and rainless clouds, promising freedom while slaves of corruption. Having known the way of righteousness and turned back, they are worse off than before, like a dog returning to its vomit, or a washed pig to the mud.
verseByVerse.theology:
Washed, Not Changed

The false teachers promise freedom while slaves of corruption. The washed sow returns to the mire because her nature was never changed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Like Balaam, they loved gain and preyed on unsteady new believers.

Now: The question is not whether you have been washed, but whether you have been changed.

verseByVerse.quote: and especially those who indulge in the lust of defiling passion and despise authority. Bold and willful, they do not tremble as they blaspheme the glorious ones, whereas angels, though greater in might and power, do not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against them before the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and especially those who indulge in the lust of defiling passion and despise authority. Bold and willful, they do not tremble as they blaspheme the glorious ones, whereas angels, though greater in might and power, do not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against them before the Lord.

And especially those who indulge in the lust of defiling passion. Key words. “Indulge” (poreuomenous, go after, walk after). “Defiling passion” (epithymia miasmou, desire of defilement, polluting lust): sexual immorality of various kinds, perhaps including perversions.

And despise authority. Key words. “Authority” (kyriotētos, lordship, dominion): either Christ’s lordship, or church authority, or angelic powers. They reject any authority over them.

Bold and willful. Key words. “Bold” (tolmētai, daring, audacious, reckless). “Willful” (authadeis, self-willed, arrogant, stubborn), as in Titus 1:7.

They do not tremble as they blaspheme the glorious ones. Key words. “Glorious ones” (doxas, glories): angelic beings, probably fallen angels or demons. The false teachers mock spiritual powers, speaking contemptuously of evil spirits, perhaps claiming that their “freedom” made them invulnerable.

Whereas angels, though greater in might and power, do not pronounce a blasphemous judgment against them before the Lord. Key words. Even holy angels, who are far more powerful, do not insult evil spirits but leave judgement to God. Jude 9 gives the example of the archangel Michael, who, disputing with the devil over Moses’ body, did not rebuke him himself but said, “The Lord rebuke you.” The false teachers are arrogant where angels are humble.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should fear demons. Christ has triumphed over them (Colossians 2:15). It means believers should not be flippant or arrogant about spiritual powers, but resist them by faith in Christ’s authority, not their own.

In a sentence. This is especially true of those who follow the corrupt desire of the flesh and despise authority. Bold and arrogant, they are not afraid to heap abuse on celestial beings; yet even angels, although they are stronger and more powerful, do not heap abuse on such beings when bringing judgement on them from the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Is there any authority you despise: God’s, the church’s, legitimate human authority? Humble yourself before God this week.

verseByVerse.quote: But these, like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be caught and destroyed, blaspheming about matters of which they are ignorant, will also be destroyed in their destruction, suffering wrong as the wage for their wrongdoing. They count it pleasure to revel in the daytime. They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their deceptions, while they feast with you. They have eyes full of adultery, insatiable for sin. They entice unsteady souls. They have hearts trained in greed. Accursed children!
verseByVerse.commentary:
But these, like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be caught and destroyed, blaspheming about matters of which they are ignorant, will also be destroyed in their destruction, suffering wrong as the wage for their wrongdoing. They count it pleasure to revel in the daytime. They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their deceptions, while they feast with you. They have eyes full of adultery, insatiable for sin. They entice unsteady souls. They have hearts trained in greed. Accursed children!

But these, like irrational animals, creatures of instinct. Key words. “Irrational” (aloga, without reason). “Creatures of instinct” (gegennēmena physika, born as natural creatures). They claim superior knowledge but behave like animals driven only by appetite (Jude 10).

Born to be caught and destroyed. Key words. Like wild animals that end in hunters’ traps.

Blaspheming about matters of which they are ignorant. Key words. They speak contemptuously of things they do not understand.

Will also be destroyed in their destruction. Key words. A wordplay: they will perish in their perishing, like animals.

Suffering wrong as the wage for their wrongdoing. Key words. Another wordplay: adikoumenoi misthon adikias, being wronged as the wage of wrong. They will receive exactly what they deserve.

They count it pleasure to revel in the daytime. Key words. “Revel” (tryphēn, luxurious indulgence). Even respectable pagans saved their partying for night (1 Thessalonians 5:7). These people indulge shamelessly in broad daylight.

They are blots and blemishes. Key words. “Blots” (spiloi, stains) and “blemishes” (mōmoi, disgraces). The opposite of Christ, the lamb “without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19), and of believers who should be “without spot or blemish” (3:14).

Reveling in their deceptions, while they feast with you. Key words. “Deceptions” (apatais; some manuscripts read agapais, love feasts, as in Jude 12). The early church’s fellowship meals, often with the Lord’s Supper. The false teachers took part, turning sacred fellowship into self-indulgence.

They have eyes full of adultery. Key words. Literally “eyes full of an adulteress”: every woman they look at is a potential conquest (Matthew 5:28).

Insatiable for sin. Key words. “Insatiable” (akatapaustous, unceasing, never resting). Sin never satisfies; it always wants more.

They entice unsteady souls. Key words. “Entice” (deleazontes, bait, lure), as in James 1:14. “Unsteady” (astēriktous, unstable, not established). New or weak believers are their targets.

They have hearts trained in greed. Key words. “Trained” (gegymnasmenēn, exercised, as in a gymnasium). They have practised greed so long they are experts at it.

Accursed children! Key words. “Accursed children” (kataras tekna, children of a curse): a Hebrew way of saying people under God’s curse.

What it does not mean. The strong language does not license believers to insult opponents casually. Peter is giving an inspired, prophetic judgement on false teachers, to warn the church.

In a sentence. But these people blaspheme in matters they do not understand. They are like unreasoning animals, creatures of instinct, born only to be caught and destroyed, and like animals they too will perish. They will be paid back with harm for the harm they have done. Their idea of pleasure is to carouse in broad daylight. They are blots and blemishes, revelling in their pleasures while they feast with you. With eyes full of adultery, they never stop sinning; they seduce the unstable; they are experts in greed, an accursed brood!

On a Tuesday. Guard your eyes and your heart this week. Sin trained becomes sin mastered; godliness trained becomes godliness mastered.

verseByVerse.quote: Forsaking the right way, they have gone astray. They have followed the way of Balaam, the son of Beor, who loved gain from wrongdoing, but was rebuked for his own transgression; a speechless donkey spoke with human voice and restrained the prophet's madness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Forsaking the right way, they have gone astray. They have followed the way of Balaam, the son of Beor, who loved gain from wrongdoing, but was rebuked for his own transgression; a speechless donkey spoke with human voice and restrained the prophet’s madness.

Forsaking the right way, they have gone astray. Key words. “Right way” (eutheian hodon, straight road). “Gone astray” (eplanēthēsan, wandered, been deceived).

They have followed the way of Balaam, the son of Beor. Key words. Balaam was hired to curse Israel for money, and his donkey spoke to stop him (Numbers 22–24). Though God prevented him from cursing Israel, Balaam later advised Balak to lead Israel into sexual immorality and idolatry at Peor (Numbers 25:1–3; 31:16; Revelation 2:14). He became the classic example of a religious teacher who sells his gift for money and leads God’s people into sin (Jude 11).

Who loved gain from wrongdoing. Key words. “Loved gain from wrongdoing” (misthon adikias ēgapēsen, loved the wages of unrighteousness), echoing verse 13. Money was Balaam’s god.

But was rebuked for his own transgression. Key words. “Rebuked” (elenxin eschen, received conviction, rebuke). “Transgression” (paranomias, lawbreaking).

A speechless donkey spoke with human voice and restrained the prophet’s madness. Key words. “Speechless” (aphōnon, voiceless). “Madness” (paraphronian, insanity, being out of one’s mind). God made a donkey speak to stop the prophet (Numbers 22:21–35). The irony: the “irrational animal” (v. 12) had more sense than the prophet, and the false teachers are like Balaam, with less sense than a donkey.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all who are paid for ministry are like Balaam. Workers deserve wages (1 Timothy 5:18). The sin is loving money and compromising truth for it.

In a sentence. They have left the straight way and wandered off to follow the way of Balaam son of Beor, who loved the wages of wickedness. But he was rebuked for his wrongdoing by a donkey, an animal without speech, who spoke with a human voice and restrained the prophet’s madness.

For worship. Ask God to keep you from loving money more than truth, and to make you open to correction, even from unexpected sources.
verseByVerse.note: Balaam was hired to curse Israel for money, and his donkey spoke to rebuke him.

verseByVerse.quote: These are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm. For them the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved. For, speaking loud boasts of folly, they entice by sensual passions of the flesh those who are barely escaping from those who live in error. They promise them freedom, but they themselves are slaves of corruption. For whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are waterless springs and mists driven by a storm. For them the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved. For, speaking loud boasts of folly, they entice by sensual passions of the flesh those who are barely escaping from those who live in error. They promise them freedom, but they themselves are slaves of corruption. For whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved.

These are waterless springs. Key words. “Springs” (pēgai, fountains). In dry lands, a spring is life. A dry spring promises water and gives nothing. False teachers promise spiritual refreshment and give nothing (Jeremiah 2:13).

And mists driven by a storm. Key words. “Mists” (homichlai, haze, fog). They look like rain clouds but are blown away without giving rain (Jude 12). All promise, no substance.

For them the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved. Key words. “Gloom of utter darkness” (ho zophos tou skotous, the blackness of darkness). The destiny of the false teachers: eternal darkness, outer darkness (Matthew 8:12; 22:13; Jude 13). “Reserved” (tetērētai, kept, perfect tense).

For, speaking loud boasts of folly. Key words. “Loud boasts” (hyperonka, swelling, inflated, bombastic words). “Folly” (mataiotētos, emptiness, futility). Impressive-sounding but empty.

They entice by sensual passions of the flesh. Key words. “Entice” (deleazousin, bait), as in verse 14. The bait is sensual pleasure.

Those who are barely escaping from those who live in error. Key words. “Barely escaping” (oligōs apopheugontas, just escaping, only a little escaping): new converts who have just left paganism. They are most vulnerable.

They promise them freedom. Key words. “Freedom” (eleutherian): probably a twisted version of Christian freedom, claiming that grace means freedom from moral rules (Galatians 5:13; 1 Peter 2:16; Romans 6:1–2).

But they themselves are slaves of corruption. Key words. “Slaves” (douloi). “Corruption” (phthoras, moral decay), as in 1:4. Those who promise freedom are themselves enslaved.

For whatever overcomes a person, to that he is enslaved. Key words. “Overcomes” (hēttētai, defeats, masters). A proverb: whatever masters you is your master (John 8:34; Romans 6:16). Sin is not freedom; it is slavery.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christian freedom is false. Christ truly sets us free (John 8:36; Galatians 5:1). But freedom is from sin, not freedom to sin.

In a sentence. These people are springs without water and mists driven by a storm. Blackest darkness is reserved for them. For they mouth empty, boastful words and, by appealing to the lustful desires of the flesh, they entice people who are just escaping from those who live in error. They promise them freedom, while they themselves are slaves of depravity, for people are slaves to whatever has mastered them.

On a Tuesday. What masters you? If anything other than Christ controls you, bring it to him for freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: For if, after they have escaped the defilements of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, the last state has become worse for them than the first. For it would have been better for them never to have known the way of righteousness than after knowing it to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. What the true proverb says has happened to them: "The dog returns to its own vomit, and the sow, after washing herself, returns to wallow in the mire."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if, after they have escaped the defilements of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, they are again entangled in them and overcome, the last state has become worse for them than the first. For it would have been better for them never to have known the way of righteousness than after knowing it to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. What the true proverb says has happened to them: “The dog returns to its own vomit, and the sow, after washing herself, returns to wallow in the mire.”

For if, after they have escaped the defilements of the world. Key words. “They”: the false teachers, and perhaps those they led astray. “Escaped” (apophygontes), as in 1:4. “Defilements” (miasmata, pollutions). They had outwardly left their former life of sin.

Through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Key words. “Knowledge” (epignōsei). They had known the gospel, understood it, perhaps professed it.

They are again entangled in them and overcome. Key words. “Entangled” (emplakentes, woven in, caught). “Overcome” (hēttōntai, defeated), as in verse 19.

The last state has become worse for them than the first. Key words. Echoing Jesus (Matthew 12:45; Luke 11:26). Having known the truth and rejected it, they are more guilty and more hardened than before.

For it would have been better for them never to have known the way of righteousness. Key words. Greater knowledge brings greater responsibility (Luke 12:47–48; Hebrews 6:4–6; 10:26–29).

Than after knowing it to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them. Key words. “Turn back” (hypostrepsai, return). “Holy commandment”: the Christian faith and way of life, delivered by the apostles (Jude 3).

What the true proverb says has happened to them. Key words. “True proverb” (alēthous paroimias).

The dog returns to its own vomit. Key words. From Proverbs 26:11. Dogs in the ancient world were scavengers, despised as unclean.

And the sow, after washing herself, returns to wallow in the mire. Key words. A popular proverb. The pig was washed on the outside, but its nature was unchanged; it went straight back to the mud. These two proverbs explain the passage: the false teachers were outwardly cleaned, but their nature was never changed. They were dogs and pigs all along, never sheep.

Where Christians differ: does this passage show that true believers can lose salvation? Verdict: The proverbs answer the question. The dog and the sow returned to filth because their nature had never been changed; they were washed outwardly but remained dogs and pigs. These people had external knowledge of Christ and outward moral reform, but never received a new nature (1:4). True believers, made partakers of the divine nature, are kept by God’s power (1 Peter 1:5) and will never finally fall (1:10). Those who return permanently to their former life show they were never truly regenerated (1 John 2:19).

What it does not mean. It does not mean a believer who sins after conversion is lost. All believers stumble (James 3:2). The issue is a settled, final return to a life of sin, rejecting the truth.

In a sentence. If they have escaped the corruption of the world by knowing our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ and are again entangled in it and overcome, they are worse off at the end than they were at the beginning. It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than to have known it and then to turn their backs on the sacred command passed on to them. Of them the proverbs are true: “A dog returns to its vomit,” and, “A sow that is washed returns to her wallowing in the mud.”

For worship. Thank God that he did not merely wash you on the outside, but gave you a new nature. Ask him to keep you from ever returning to the mire.

2.theology: The chapter's controlling theological question is the nature of apostasy. Can a person who has genuinely known Christ fall finally away? The Reformed answer: those truly regenerate will persevere (John 10:28–29; Rom 8:38–39). But the visible church contains those who participate in covenant privileges without possessing covenant life — and it is these who can experience the knowledge described in v. 20 and still return to their former state. The dog and pig proverbs define the boundary: the animal's nature is unchanged. External reformation without regeneration leads to greater corruption. This is not a loophole in the doctrine of perseverance; it is the doctrine's honest context.
2.examples: The Balaam portrait (vv. 15–16) gives the congregation diagnostic tools. The false teacher's test is not doctrinal sophistication but financial transparency: What does this teacher gain from what he teaches? Is the teaching shaped by what people want to hear (and therefore what they will pay to hear)? Balaam was a genuine prophet whose gift was real — but the gift became a commodity. The test of authentic ministry is not whether the gifts are real but whether the teacher loves the Lord more than the wages.

3.title: The Day That Is Coming
3.overview:
The last chapter is the letter’s goal. The false teachers are dangerous because they attack the hope of Christ’s return, and with it the reason for holy living. If no day is coming, why be holy?

Peter answers in three steps. The world has not always continued as it was: God’s word created it and judged it by the flood, and the same word holds it now for judgment. God is not slow, but patient, giving time for repentance. And the day will come suddenly and lay everything bare. So the question is not “When?” but “What sort of people ought you to be?” The letter ends: grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever.
3.text: <sup>1</sup>This is now the second letter that I am writing to you, beloved. In both of them I am stirring up your sincere mind by way of reminder,<sup>2</sup>that you should remember the predictions of the holy prophets and the commandment of the Lord and Savior through your apostles,<sup>3</sup>knowing this first of all, that scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing, following their own sinful desires.<sup>4</sup>They will say, "Where is the promise of his coming?
