For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation."<sup>5</sup>For they deliberately overlook this fact, that the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God,<sup>6</sup>and that by means of these the world that then existed was deluged with water and perished.<sup>7</sup>But by the same word the heavens and earth that now exist are stored up for fire, being kept until the day of judgment and destruction of the ungodly.<sup>8</sup>But do not overlook this one fact, beloved, that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.<sup>9</sup>The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.<sup>10</sup>But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and then the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the heavenly bodies will be burned up and dissolved, and the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed.<sup>11</sup>Since all these things are thus to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness,<sup>12</sup>waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God, because of which the heavens will be set on fire and dissolved, and the heavenly bodies will melt as they burn!<sup>13</sup>But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.<sup>14</sup>Therefore, beloved, since you are waiting for these, be diligent to be found by him without spot or blemish, and at peace.<sup>15</sup>And count the patience of our Lord as salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given him,<sup>16</sup>as he does in all his letters when he speaks in them of these matters. There are some things in them that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures.<sup>17</sup>You therefore, beloved, knowing this beforehand, take care that you are not carried away with the error of lawless people and lose your own stability.<sup>18</sup>But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Scoffers and the Day
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter writes to remind them of the prophets and the apostles’ teaching. Scoffers will come, following their desires, saying, “Where is the promise of his coming?” They choose to forget that God’s word created the world and destroyed it by the flood, and that the same word now holds the heavens and earth for the fire of judgment. With the Lord a day is as a thousand years. He is not slow but patient, wanting all to come to repentance. And the day will come like a thief.
verseByVerse.theology:
Not Slowness but Patience

The world has not always continued as it was: God's word made it and judged it by the flood. The Lord is not slow but patient, and the day will come like a thief.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Scoffers pointed to the death of the first generation as proof that nothing was coming.

Now: The delay is mercy; the right response is repentance, not argument about the timetable.

verseByVerse.quote: This is now the second letter that I am writing to you, beloved. In both of them I am stirring up your sincere mind by way of reminder, that you should remember the predictions of the holy prophets and the commandment of the Lord and Savior through your apostles,
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is now the second letter that I am writing to you, beloved. In both of them I am stirring up your sincere mind by way of reminder, that you should remember the predictions of the holy prophets and the commandment of the Lord and Savior through your apostles,

Meaning first. 2 Peter 3 answers the false teachers’ denial of Christ’s return and calls believers to holy living as they wait. Peter writes to remind them of the prophets’ predictions and the apostles’ teaching (vv. 1–2). Scoffers will come, living for their desires and mocking the promise of his coming and claiming that nothing has changed since creation (vv. 3–4). But they deliberately ignore that God created the world by his word and judged it once by water; by the same word the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire on the day of judgement (vv. 5–7). God does not measure time as we do: a day is like a thousand years to him; his apparent delay is patience, not wanting any to perish but all to come to repentance (vv. 8–9). The day of the Lord will come like a thief; the heavens will pass away, the elements will melt, and the earth and its works will be exposed (v. 10). Since everything will be dissolved, believers should live holy and godly lives, looking forward to and hastening that day, and to new heavens and a new earth where righteousness dwells (vv. 11–13). So they should be diligent to be found spotless and at peace, regarding the Lord’s patience as salvation, as Paul also wrote, whose letters the unstable twist as they do the other Scriptures (vv. 14–16). The letter ends with a final warning not to be carried away by error, and a final command: grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, to whom be glory now and forever (vv. 17–18).

This is now the second letter that I am writing to you, beloved. Key words. The earlier letter is most likely 1 Peter. “Beloved” (agapētoi): used four times in this chapter (vv. 1, 8, 14, 17), a warm contrast with the harsh words about false teachers.

In both of them I am stirring up your sincere mind by way of reminder. Key words. “Stirring up” (diegeirō, rousing, waking), as in 1:13. “Sincere” (eilikrinē, pure, unmixed, tested by sunlight, as pottery was held up to the sun to check for cracks). “Mind” (dianoian, understanding). Unlike the false teachers, the readers have pure minds, but they still need reminding.

That you should remember the predictions of the holy prophets. Key words. “Predictions” (proeirēmenōn rhēmatōn, words spoken beforehand). The Old Testament prophets foretold the Day of the Lord, judgement and new creation (Isaiah 65:17; 66:22; Joel 2; Daniel 7; 12).

And the commandment of the Lord and Savior through your apostles. Key words. “Commandment” (entolēs): the apostolic teaching, including Christ’s promise to return. “Through your apostles”: the apostles are Christ’s mouthpieces. Peter places the apostles’ teaching alongside the Old Testament prophets as equally authoritative. The two together, Old Testament and New Testament, form the foundation (Ephesians 2:20).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the apostles invented new commandments. They delivered what Christ commanded (Matthew 28:20).

In a sentence. Dear friends, this is now my second letter to you. I have written both of them as reminders to stimulate you to wholesome thinking. I want you to recall the words spoken in the past by the holy prophets and the command given by our Lord and Saviour through your apostles.

For worship. Thank God for the prophets and apostles, whose words you hold in your Bible. Let them stir your mind today.
verseByVerse.note: The earlier letter is most likely 1 Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: knowing this first of all, that scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing, following their own sinful desires. They will say, "Where is the promise of his coming? For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
knowing this first of all, that scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing, following their own sinful desires. They will say, “Where is the promise of his coming? For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation.”

Knowing this first of all. Key words. As in 1:20.

That scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing. Key words. “Scoffers” (empaiktai, mockers, ridiculers). “With scoffing” (en empaigmonē, in mockery): a Hebrew-style emphasis. “Last days”: the whole period since Christ’s first coming (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2; Jude 18). The scoffers were already present in Peter’s day.

Following their own sinful desires. Key words. The link between denying judgement and indulging desires. If there is no coming judgement, there is no reason to restrain oneself. Their theology serves their lusts.

They will say, Where is the promise of his coming? Key words. “Promise of his coming” (hē epangelia tēs parousias autou): Jesus’ promise to return (John 14:3; Acts 1:11). The mocking question echoes Old Testament scoffers (Psalm 42:3; Malachi 2:17).

For ever since the fathers fell asleep. Key words. “The fathers”: probably the first generation of Christians, who had died, or perhaps the Old Testament patriarchs. “Fell asleep” (ekoimēthēsan): died, a common Christian euphemism (1 Thessalonians 4:13–15). Decades had passed; Christ had not come.

All things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation. Key words. “Continuing” (diamenei, remain unchanged). The argument from uniformity: the world goes on as it always has; God does not intervene; there will be no judgement. A view still common today.

What it does not mean. It does not mean honest questions about the timing of Christ’s return are scoffing. Scoffing is mocking unbelief that rejects God’s promise in order to justify sin.

In a sentence. Above all, you must understand that in the last days scoffers will come, scoffing and following their own evil desires. They will say, “Where is this ‘coming’ he promised? Ever since our ancestors died, everything goes on as it has since the beginning of creation.”

On a Tuesday. Have you ever been mocked for believing Christ will return? Don’t be shaken; Scripture said it would happen.

verseByVerse.quote: For they deliberately overlook this fact, that the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God, and that by means of these the world that then existed was deluged with water and perished. But by the same word the heavens and earth that now exist are stored up for fire, being kept until the day of judgment and destruction of the ungodly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For they deliberately overlook this fact, that the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God, and that by means of these the world that then existed was deluged with water and perished. But by the same word the heavens and earth that now exist are stored up for fire, being kept until the day of judgment and destruction of the ungodly.

For they deliberately overlook this fact. Key words. “Deliberately overlook” (lanthanei thelontas, it escapes their notice because they want it to, they wilfully forget). Their ignorance is chosen (Romans 1:18–21).

That the heavens existed long ago, and the earth was formed out of water and through water by the word of God. Key words. The first fact they ignore: creation. God made the world by his word (Genesis 1; Hebrews 11:3). “Out of water and through water”: in Genesis 1, the earth emerged from the waters (1:2, 6–10). The world is not self-existent or eternal; it depends on God’s word.

And that by means of these the world that then existed was deluged with water and perished. Key words. The second fact they ignore: the flood. “By means of these” (di’ hōn): by water and the word. “Deluged” (kataklystheis, flooded; from which comes “cataclysm”). “Perished” (apōleto, was destroyed). The world did not continue unchanged; God judged it once. The scoffers’ claim that “all things continue” is false.

But by the same word the heavens and earth that now exist are stored up for fire. Key words. “Same word”: God’s word that created and judged will judge again. “Stored up” (tethēsaurismenoi, reserved, treasured up). “For fire”: the next judgement will be by fire, not water (Genesis 9:11; Isaiah 66:15–16; Malachi 4:1; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–8).

Being kept until the day of judgment and destruction of the ungodly. Key words. “Kept” (tēroumenoi, guarded, preserved). God is holding the present world until judgement. “Destruction” (apōleias, perdition, ruin). For the ungodly, eternal ruin.

What it does not mean. “Destruction” does not mean annihilation of the ungodly. Scripture describes their punishment as eternal and conscious (Matthew 25:46; Revelation 14:11; 20:10). The word means ruin, loss of all that makes existence good.

In a sentence. But they deliberately forget that long ago by God’s word the heavens came into being and the earth was formed out of water and by water. By these waters also the world of that time was deluged and destroyed. By the same word the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire, being kept for the day of judgement and destruction of the ungodly.

For worship. Praise the God whose word created and judged the world, and who holds it now until the day of judgement. Trust his word.

verseByVerse.quote: But do not overlook this one fact, beloved, that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But do not overlook this one fact, beloved, that with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.

But do not overlook this one fact, beloved. Key words. “Do not overlook” (mē lanthanetō, do not let it escape you), the same word as verse 5. The scoffers deliberately forget; believers must not.

That with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. Key words. Echoing Psalm 90:4: “A thousand years in your sight are but as yesterday when it is past.” God is not bound by time as we are. He is eternal. What seems a long delay to us is nothing to him. Equally, he can accomplish in a day what would take us a thousand years. The point: we must not judge God’s faithfulness by our timetable.

Where Christians differ: does this verse teach a thousand-year day or a millennial scheme? Some have used this verse to calculate the timing of Christ’s return, such as six thousand years of history followed by a thousand-year millennium. Verdict: The verse is not a formula for calculation; it teaches that God’s perspective on time differs from ours. It warns against date-setting, not encourages it (Matthew 24:36; Acts 1:7). It gives no support to elaborate millennial timetables.

What it does not mean. It does not mean time is meaningless to God, or that “day” in Scripture always means a thousand years. It means God sees time from eternity, and his promises are not delayed by our standards.

In a sentence. But do not forget this one thing, dear friends: with the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day.

For worship. When God seems slow, remember: he sees all time at once. Trust his perfect timing.

parallels.desc: a thousand years in your sight are but as yesterday

verseByVerse.quote: The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.

The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness. Key words. “Slow” (bradynei, delay, loiter). “As some count slowness”: the scoffers interpret delay as failure. But the delay has a purpose.

But is patient toward you. Key words. “Patient” (makrothymei, long-suffering, slow to anger). “Toward you” (eis hymas): the readers, God’s beloved people (v. 1), the chosen (1 Peter 1:1). God delays for their sake.

Not wishing that any should perish. Key words. “Wishing” (boulomenos, willing, desiring). “Perish” (apolesthai, be destroyed). God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 18:23, 32; 33:11).

But that all should reach repentance. Key words. “Reach” (chōrēsai, come to, make room for). “Repentance” (metanoian, change of mind and direction). God’s patience gives time for repentance (Romans 2:4).

Where Christians differ: if God wishes all to repent, why are not all saved? Arminians read this verse as showing that God wills every individual to be saved and that human choice makes the difference; universalists as showing that all will eventually be saved. Verdict: The context helps: God is patient “toward you,” addressing believers, the beloved, the elect. The delay of Christ’s return is so that all of God’s people, including those not yet converted, may come to repentance before the end. When the last of the elect has been brought in, Christ will return. At the same time, Scripture teaches that God sincerely desires the repentance of all sinners in the sense that he delights in repentance and offers the gospel freely to all (Ezekiel 33:11; 1 Timothy 2:4), while he has also sovereignly chosen to save some and not all. These two truths, God’s revealed desire and his decreed purpose, are both taught, and must both be held. Universalism contradicts the next verse and the clear teaching of eternal judgement.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is unable to accomplish what he wants. It means his patience serves his purpose of bringing his people to repentance.

In a sentence. The Lord is not slow in keeping his promise, as some understand slowness. Instead he is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish, but everyone to come to repentance.

For worship. Thank God for his patience with you, which gave you time to repent. Pray for someone who has not yet come to repentance.

verseByVerse.quote: But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and then the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the heavenly bodies will be burned up and dissolved, and the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and then the heavens will pass away with a roar, and the heavenly bodies will be burned up and dissolved, and the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed.

But the day of the Lord will come like a thief. Key words. “Day of the Lord”: the Old Testament term for God’s great day of judgement and salvation (Joel 2:31; Amos 5:18–20; Zephaniah 1:14–18), now identified with Christ’s return. “Like a thief”: suddenly, unexpectedly, without warning (Matthew 24:43; 1 Thessalonians 5:2; Revelation 16:15). Not secretly, but unexpectedly. Delay does not mean it will not come.

And then the heavens will pass away with a roar. Key words. “Pass away” (pareleusontai, go by, disappear). “With a roar” (rhoizēdon, with a rushing noise, a whizzing sound, like an arrow or a crackling fire). Dramatic, sudden, audible.

And the heavenly bodies will be burned up and dissolved. Key words. “Heavenly bodies” (stoicheia, elements): either the basic elements of the physical world, or the sun, moon and stars (Isaiah 34:4). “Burned up” (kausoumena, burning with intense heat). “Dissolved” (lythēsetai, loosed, broken apart). The present order will be destroyed by fire.

And the earth and the works that are done on it will be exposed. Key words. “Exposed” (heurethēsetai, will be found, laid bare, discovered). Everything will be brought into the open before God’s judgement (1 Corinthians 3:13; Hebrews 4:13). Nothing will be hidden.

Textual note. The manuscripts differ at the end of this verse. The oldest read “will be found” or “exposed” (heurethēsetai); later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “will be burned up” (katakaēsetai); some read “will not be found.” The more difficult reading, “will be found,” is most likely original, meaning laid bare before God’s judgement.

Where Christians differ: is the day of the Lord a single event? Dispensationalists often separate a secret rapture of the church from a later visible return, and place a thousand-year earthly kingdom between Christ’s return and the final judgement and new creation. Verdict: Peter places Christ’s coming, the day of the Lord, the judgement of the ungodly, and the dissolution of the present heavens and earth together in one great event, followed by the new heavens and new earth (vv. 7, 10, 12–13). This fits the amillennial understanding: one visible return of Christ, at which the dead are raised, all are judged, and creation is renewed. There is no secret rapture and no intervening earthly millennium.

What it does not mean. It does not necessarily mean the universe will be annihilated and a new one created from nothing. Scripture speaks of the renewal of creation (Romans 8:19–21; Matthew 19:28; Acts 3:21). The fire purifies and transforms, like a refining fire, removing all that is sinful and corrupt.

In a sentence. But the day of the Lord will come like a thief. The heavens will disappear with a roar; the elements will be destroyed by fire, and the earth and everything done in it will be laid bare.

On a Tuesday. If Christ came today, what would be exposed in your life? Live in readiness, as one who will give account.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–18 — New Heavens, and the Last Command
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Since the present world will be dissolved and everything exposed before God, Peter asks what kind of people believers should be, and answers: holy and devoted to God, as they wait for the day of God and even hasten it. On that day the heavens will be set ablaze and dissolved, but believers look forward, as God promised, to new heavens and a new earth where righteousness is at home. So while they wait they should make every effort to be found by him at peace, spotless and blameless, and regard the Lord’s patience as an opportunity for salvation, as Paul also wrote with the wisdom God gave him, though some of his letters contain things hard to understand that unstable and untaught people twist, as they twist the rest of Scripture, to their own ruin. Forewarned, they must guard against being carried off by the error of the lawless, and instead grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, to whom be glory now and for ever.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Answer to Error Is Growth

Since everything will be laid bare, live in holiness and godliness while waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells. The last command is to grow in the grace and knowledge of Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Peter called Paul a beloved brother and counted his letters among the Scriptures.

Now: A growing believer is far harder to uproot than one who is merely on guard.

verseByVerse.quote: Since all these things are thus to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness, waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God, because of which the heavens will be set on fire and dissolved, and the heavenly bodies will melt as they burn! But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since all these things are thus to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness, waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God, because of which the heavens will be set on fire and dissolved, and the heavenly bodies will melt as they burn! But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.

Since all these things are thus to be dissolved. Key words. “Dissolved” (lyomenōn, being loosed, present tense: as good as dissolving already). The present world is temporary.

What sort of people ought you to be in lives of holiness and godliness. Key words. “What sort” (potapous, what kind, how excellent). “Holiness” (hagiais anastrophais, holy ways of life, plural: in every area). “Godliness” (eusebeiais, plural: acts of godliness). Eschatology is not for speculation but for transformation. Belief in Christ’s return shapes holy living (1 John 3:2–3).

Waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of God. Key words. “Waiting for” (prosdokōntas, expecting, looking for eagerly). “Hastening” (speudontas, hurrying, speeding up, or eagerly desiring). Believers can, in some sense, hasten the day: by holy living, prayer (“Your kingdom come,” Matthew 6:10), and evangelism, which brings in the elect whose conversion the Lord awaits (v. 9; Matthew 24:14). God has ordained the means as well as the end.

Because of which the heavens will be set on fire and dissolved, and the heavenly bodies will melt as they burn! Key words. “Melt” (tēketai), as in Isaiah 34:4 (Greek) and Micah 1:4.

But according to his promise we are waiting for new heavens and a new earth. Key words. “According to his promise” (kata to epangelma autou): Isaiah 65:17; 66:22. “New” (kainous, new in quality, renewed, fresh). Not merely a new universe in time, but a transformed one in kind (Revelation 21:1–5; Romans 8:19–21).

In which righteousness dwells. Key words. “Dwells” (katoikei, settles down, makes its permanent home). In the present world, righteousness is a stranger; in the new creation, it will be at home. No more sin, injustice, evil or death (Revelation 21:4, 27).

What it does not mean. “Hastening” does not mean we control God’s timetable or can force his hand. It means God uses his people’s prayers, holiness and witness in bringing about his purposes. Nor does a new creation mean the present world is worthless; it will be renewed, not discarded.

In a sentence. Since everything will be destroyed in this way, what kind of people ought you to be? You ought to live holy and godly lives as you look forward to the day of God and speed its coming. That day will bring about the destruction of the heavens by fire, and the elements will melt in the heat. But in keeping with his promise we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness is at home.

For worship. Pray “Your kingdom come” today, and long for the new creation where righteousness dwells.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, beloved, since you are waiting for these, be diligent to be found by him without spot or blemish, and at peace. And count the patience of our Lord as salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given him, as he does in all his letters when he speaks in them of these matters. There are some things in them that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, beloved, since you are waiting for these, be diligent to be found by him without spot or blemish, and at peace. And count the patience of our Lord as salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given him, as he does in all his letters when he speaks in them of these matters. There are some things in them that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures.

Therefore, beloved, since you are waiting for these. Key words. “Waiting” (prosdokōntes), as in verse 12.

Be diligent to be found by him without spot or blemish, and at peace. Key words. “Be diligent” (spoudasate, make every effort), as in 1:5, 10. “Found” (heurethēnai), as in verse 10: when everything is exposed, be found in a good condition. “Without spot” (aspiloi) and “blemish” (amōmētoi): like Christ, the spotless Lamb (1 Peter 1:19), and the opposite of the false teachers, who are “blots and blemishes” (2:13). “At peace” (en eirēnē): at peace with God through Christ (Romans 5:1), and with one another.

And count the patience of our Lord as salvation. Key words. “Count” (hēgeisthe, regard, consider). The scoffers count it slowness (v. 9); believers count it salvation: every day of delay is a day of grace for more people to repent.

Just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given him. Key words. “Beloved brother”: despite Paul’s public rebuke of Peter (Galatians 2:11–14), Peter speaks warmly of him. “Wisdom given him”: inspired wisdom, from God. Paul also taught about God’s patience leading to repentance (Romans 2:4; 9:22) and Christ’s return.

As he does in all his letters when he speaks in them of these matters. Key words. “All his letters”: Peter knew a collection of Paul’s letters, already circulating among the churches.

There are some things in them that are hard to understand. Key words. “Hard to understand” (dysnoēta, difficult to grasp). An honest admission, from an apostle no less. Some of Paul’s teaching, perhaps on grace, freedom, election, or the last things, requires careful thought.

Which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction. Key words. “Ignorant” (amatheis, untaught, unlearned). “Unstable” (astēriktoi, not established), as in 2:14. “Twist” (strebloūsin, wrench, distort, torture, as on a rack). The false teachers twisted Paul’s teaching on grace into a licence for immorality (Romans 3:8; 6:1). “To their own destruction”: misusing Scripture leads to ruin.

As they do the other Scriptures. Key words. “Other Scriptures” (tas loipas graphas). Peter already counts Paul’s letters among “the Scriptures,” alongside the Old Testament. A remarkable early testimony to the recognition of the New Testament as inspired Scripture, within the apostolic generation itself.

What it does not mean. “Hard to understand” does not mean Scripture is unclear in its main message, or that ordinary believers cannot read it. The gospel is clear (Psalm 19:7). It means some passages require careful, humble study, and that we must not twist them to suit ourselves.

In a sentence. So then, dear friends, since you are looking forward to this, make every effort to be found spotless, blameless and at peace with him. Bear in mind that our Lord’s patience means salvation, just as our dear brother Paul also wrote to you with the wisdom God gave him. He writes the same way in all his letters, speaking in them of these matters. His letters contain some things that are hard to understand, which ignorant and unstable people distort, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction.

On a Tuesday. When you read a hard passage of Scripture, study it humbly, in context, with good help. Never twist it to say what you want.

verseByVerse.quote: You therefore, beloved, knowing this beforehand, take care that you are not carried away with the error of lawless people and lose your own stability. But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You therefore, beloved, knowing this beforehand, take care that you are not carried away with the error of lawless people and lose your own stability. But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.

You therefore, beloved, knowing this beforehand. Key words. “Knowing beforehand” (proginōskontes, being forewarned). Forewarned is forearmed.

Take care that you are not carried away with the error of lawless people. Key words. “Take care” (phylassesthe, guard yourselves, be on guard). “Carried away” (synapachthentes, led away together with, swept along with), the word used of Barnabas being carried away by Peter’s hypocrisy (Galatians 2:13). “Error” (planē, wandering, deception). “Lawless” (athesmōn, unprincipled), as of the Sodomites (2:7).

And lose your own stability. Key words. “Lose” (ekpesēte, fall from). “Stability” (stērigmou, firmness, steadfastness), from the same root as “established” (1:12) and “unstable” (v. 16; 2:14). The opposite of the unstable who twist Scripture.

But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Key words. “Grow” (auxanete, keep growing, present tense). The best defence against error is not merely avoiding it but growing in truth. “Grace”: God’s unmerited favour, experienced more and more deeply. “Knowledge”: personal knowledge of Christ (1:2–3, 8). The letter ends where it began (1:2).

To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen. Key words. “To him”: Jesus Christ. A doxology addressed to Christ, offering him the glory due to God alone (Isaiah 42:8). A final testimony to his deity. “Day of eternity” (hēmeran aiōnos): the eternal day that begins at his return and never ends.

What it does not mean. “Lose your stability” does not mean true believers can finally fall away. Peter has said they will never fall if they grow (1:10). The warning is one of God’s means to keep them standing.

In a sentence. Therefore, dear friends, since you have been forewarned, be on your guard so that you may not be carried away by the error of the lawless and fall from your secure position. But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. To him be glory both now and for ever! Amen.

For worship. Give glory to Jesus Christ today, now and forever. And ask him to help you grow in his grace and in knowing him.

3.theology:
Uniformitarianism and the Word of God: Peter's refutation of the scoffers in vv. 5–7 is a model of theological apologetics. The uniformitarians claim that the world operates by consistent natural processes. Peter grants the observation and then shows that the historical record — the record the uniformitarians themselves appeal to — contains two catastrophic interruptions of the very uniformity they invoke: creation and the flood. Both were brought about by the word of God. The same word that did those things has spoken again, and the third act — the fire — is as certain as the first two. The apologist who begins with Scripture's own historical witness is standing on solid ground.

Divine patience and the will of God in salvation: Verse 9 is one of the great texts on the scope of God's salvific will: 'not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.' Reformed theology reads this in its literary context: 'toward you' — the elect community. The 'all' is the full complement of those for whom God's patience is being exercised — all who will come to repentance within the span of his patience. This is not universalism (the Day will still come and shut the door), and it is not a contradiction of election (God's patience is itself the means by which the elect are gathered). It is the breathtaking truth that the apparent delay of the parousia is not divine procrastination — it is divine love, actively gathering those who are his.

New creation as promise: The new heavens and new earth of verse 13 is the eschatological horizon of the entire epistle — and of the entire New Testament. Herman Bavinck's axiom — grace restores nature — finds its ultimate expression here: the fire does not destroy the creation but purifies it; the new creation is this creation glorified, the world God made very good and will make even better. Anthony Hoekema's The Bible and the Future demonstrates that the new earth is not a replacement but a renewal — which is why Christian hope is not escapism but engagement: the world we tend and serve and love matters eternally, because it is the world God intends to redeem.
3.examples:
Then: The scoffers' question — 'Where is the promise of his coming?' — has been asked in every generation. The first generation of believers died; the second, the third, the hundredth. Each generation has faced the apparent delay, and the temptation to conclude that the promise was empty. Peter's answer remains the same across every generation: God is not slow. He is patient. His patience is not weakness — it is mercy in motion, gathering those who are still to be gathered before the door closes. Every generation of Christians lives in the overlap of promise and fulfilment, patience and urgency.

Now: 'What sort of people ought you to be?' (v. 11) is the most searching pastoral question the letter asks, and it lands as heavily today as it did in the first century. The return of Christ has not yet come — but it is coming, and it is certain. The question is not about calculation but about formation. The person who genuinely believes the Day is coming will live differently: with moral seriousness, with urgency about the gospel, with detachment from the world's false securities, with eager longing for righteousness. The Christian who has domesticated eschatology into a theological opinion without ethical bite has not yet let 2 Peter 3 do its work. Let it. Grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. That is the whole assignment — and it will last exactly until the Day of eternity.
